title: Chapter 8 Drill: Benign Gynecology: Bleeding, Pain, Early Pregnancy, and Pelvic Masses

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman treated for pelvic infection reports sharp right upper quadrant pain that worsens with breathing. Liver enzymes are normal, and ultrasonography of the gallbladder is normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: Acute cholecystitis
Acute viral hepatitis
Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome)
Right lower lobe pneumonia
items.explanation: Pleuritic right upper quadrant pain with pelvic infection suggests perihepatitis, caused by spread of gonococcal or chlamydial infection to the liver capsule, sometimes with violin-string adhesions. Liver enzymes are usually normal. Cholecystitis would show gallbladder findings on imaging. Viral hepatitis raises transaminases. Pneumonia would produce cough and abnormal chest imaging. Treatment is the standard pelvic infection regimen.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has tried to conceive for 12 months. Her partner has normal semen analysis, and saline infusion sonography shows a 4 cm intramural fibroid that does not distort the endometrial cavity. Her tubes are patent. What is the best management?
options: Myomectomy before any attempt at conception
Proceed with fertility treatment without myomectomy
Uterine artery embolization
Six months of GnRH agonist therapy
items.explanation: Intramural fibroids that do not distort the cavity have little effect on fertility, and routine removal does not clearly improve pregnancy rates, while surgery adds risks such as adhesions and a uterine scar. Embolization is not recommended when pregnancy is desired. A GnRH agonist only shrinks fibroids temporarily and delays conception while age-related fertility decline continues.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 9 weeks by ultrasonography requests medical abortion. She has no contraindications and is hemodynamically normal. Which regimen is evidence-based?
options: Mifepristone 200 mg orally, then misoprostol 800 mcg buccally 24 to 48 hours later
Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscularly, then misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally in 5 days
Misoprostol 800 mcg buccally, then mifepristone 200 mg orally 48 hours later
Mifepristone 600 mg orally as the only medication
items.explanation: The standard regimen is mifepristone 200 mg orally followed by misoprostol 800 mcg, usually buccal, in 24 to 48 hours. Mifepristone blocks progesterone and primes the uterus to respond. Methotrexate regimens are slower and less effective. Reversing the order loses the priming effect. Mifepristone alone has a lower success rate and is not the recommended regimen.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 6 weeks has a stable, unruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy of 2.5 cm with a human chorionic gonadotropin level of 2,400 mIU/mL. Which finding would make methotrexate inappropriate?
options: A human chorionic gonadotropin of 2,400 mIU/mL
A tubal mass of 2.5 cm
Rh-negative blood type
Hypotension with free fluid in the hepatorenal space
items.explanation: Methotrexate is for hemodynamically stable women with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy. Hypotension with free fluid in the hepatorenal pouch indicates rupture and hemoperitoneum, so surgery is needed. A level of 2,400 is well within the usual range, and a 2.5 cm mass is below the 3.5 cm limit. Rh-negative status needs immune globulin but does not exclude methotrexate.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has abdominal distension. Imaging shows a 9 cm solid adnexal mass, ascites, and a right pleural effusion. After the mass is removed, the ascites and effusion resolve completely. Which tumor was most likely removed?
options: Ovarian fibroma
Serous cystadenoma
Granulosa cell tumor
Dysgerminoma
items.explanation: A solid benign ovarian fibroma with ascites and a right pleural effusion that resolve after resection defines Meigs syndrome. The fluid is a transudate and clears once the tumor is gone. Serous cystadenomas are cystic. Granulosa cell tumors produce estrogen and cause bleeding. Dysgerminomas affect younger women and are malignant. Persistent fluid after surgery would argue against a fibroma.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has mild left lower quadrant pain and light spotting. She is hemodynamically stable. Her serum hCG is 1,800 mIU/mL, and transvaginal ultrasonography shows an empty uterus and normal adnexa with no free fluid. What is the best next step?
options: Administer methotrexate today
Repeat the hCG level in 48 hours
Perform dilation and curettage
Proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy
items.explanation: This is a pregnancy of unknown location in a stable patient with a level below the discriminatory range, so it is too early to distinguish an early intrauterine pregnancy from an ectopic or failing pregnancy. A repeat level at 48 hours shows the trend. Methotrexate risks harming a viable pregnancy. Curettage or laparoscopy is premature without evidence of a failing pregnancy or instability.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 2 years of chronic lower abdominal pain localized to a small area. When she lifts her head and tenses her abdominal muscles during palpation of the tender spot, the pain increases. What is the most likely source?
options: Visceral pain from endometriosis
Adenomyosis
Anterior abdominal wall myofascial pain
An ovarian remnant
items.explanation: Pain that stays the same or increases with abdominal wall tensing, a positive Carnett sign, localizes the source to the abdominal wall, for example from nerve entrapment or myofascial trigger points. Visceral pain tends to diminish when the muscles tense and protect the viscera. Endometriosis, adenomyosis, and ovarian remnant produce deeper pain and are usually cyclic or accompanied by a mass.

items.stem: A 47-year-old G2P2 woman with a body mass index of 38 has had irregular, heavy bleeding for 6 months. Pregnancy test is negative and hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL. Pelvic examination is normal. What is the best next step?
options: A trial of tranexamic acid before any testing
Placement of a levonorgestrel intrauterine device without sampling
Repeat thyroid and prolactin testing in 3 months
Endometrial biopsy
items.explanation: Women aged 45 or older with abnormal bleeding, and younger women with prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure such as obesity, need endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia or cancer before treatment. Medical therapy such as tranexamic acid or a hormonal device may be started once sampling is done. Delaying evaluation for repeat hormone testing risks missing neoplasia in a high-risk patient.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 8 weeks by dates passed clots and tissue at home with cramping, and bleeding is now minimal. The cervical os is closed. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a thin endometrial stripe and no gestational sac. What is the diagnosis?
options: Incomplete abortion
Complete spontaneous abortion
Threatened abortion
Missed abortion
items.explanation: Passage of tissue followed by settling pain and bleeding, a closed os, and an empty uterus with a thin stripe indicate complete abortion, assuming an intrauterine pregnancy was known or hCG falls appropriately. Incomplete abortion shows retained products and an open os. Threatened abortion has bleeding with a closed os and a viable embryo. Missed abortion has a nonviable embryo retained without expulsion.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has fever of 38.6 C, lower abdominal pain, and a 5 cm tubo-ovarian abscess on ultrasonography. She is vomiting and has failed to improve on oral therapy. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Admission for intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
Outpatient oral antibiotics with reassessment at 72 hours
Immediate hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Intramuscular ceftriaxone once with discharge to home
items.explanation: A tubo-ovarian abscess is a complication of pelvic infection needing inpatient parenteral therapy with coverage for anaerobes, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. Most respond within 48 to 72 hours, and drainage is added for failure or large abscesses. Outpatient oral therapy and a single injection are inadequate in a febrile, vomiting patient. Radical surgery is reserved for rupture or sepsis.

items.stem: A 36-year-old G3P2012 woman is hemodynamically stable at 6 weeks with an unruptured 2.5 cm ectopic pregnancy and an hCG of 3,000 mIU/mL. Liver and renal function are normal. Which additional finding would make methotrexate contraindicated?
options: A prior ectopic pregnancy treated surgically 4 years ago
An unruptured mass measuring 2.5 cm in diameter
She is currently breastfeeding her infant
A serum hCG level of 3,000 mIU/mL at presentation
items.explanation: Breastfeeding is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate, along with hemodynamic instability, rupture, hepatic or renal disease, and immunodeficiency. A previous ectopic pregnancy does not preclude medical therapy. A mass under 3.5 cm and an hCG below 5,000 mIU/mL are favorable features that predict success. The patient would need surgery or a different plan if she continues nursing.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman became pregnant 8 months after a myomectomy in which the surgeon entered the endometrial cavity through a deep intramural fibroid bed. She is now at 34 weeks. What is the best plan for delivery?
options: Induction of labor at 41 weeks
Planned cesarean delivery at 37 to 38 weeks before labor
Spontaneous labor with a trial of labor and oxytocin augmentation
Cesarean delivery after the onset of labor at term
items.explanation: After a myomectomy that enters the cavity or involves most of the myometrial thickness, uterine rupture can occur before or during labor, so planned cesarean delivery before labor onset is advised, generally at 37 to 38 weeks. Trial of labor or induction exposes the scar to contractions and prolonged gestation. Waiting for labor risks rupture, which is why scheduled delivery is preferred.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman with fibroid-related heavy bleeding starts an oral GnRH antagonist combined with estradiol and a progestin. Which adverse effect limits the recommended duration of this therapy?
options: Hepatic fibrosis
Endometrial hyperplasia
Loss of bone mineral density
Nephrolithiasis
items.explanation: Oral GnRH antagonist combination products suppress ovarian estrogen and, despite add-back therapy, can reduce bone mineral density, so use is limited to about 24 months and bone density may be monitored. Hepatic fibrosis and kidney stones are not characteristic limiting effects. The progestin in the combination protects the endometrium, so hyperplasia is not the concern that restricts duration.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl with polycystic ovary syndrome has had irregular menses and occasional heavy bleeding. Under the PALM-COEIN classification, which category best describes the cause of her bleeding?
options: Ovulatory dysfunction
Coagulopathy
Endometrial disorder
Iatrogenic cause
items.explanation: In the PALM-COEIN system, structural causes are polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, and malignancy or hyperplasia, and the nonstructural causes are coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, and not yet classified. Irregular cycles with anovulation from polycystic ovary syndrome are ovulatory dysfunction. Coagulopathy would show mucosal bleeding. Iatrogenic bleeding follows medications or devices, and endometrial causes involve local lining defects.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a 5 cm unilocular simple ovarian cyst found incidentally on ultrasound. She is asymptomatic, premenopausal, and has normal vital signs. What is the best management?
options: Immediate laparoscopic cystectomy to obtain a diagnosis
CA 125 testing followed by immediate hysterectomy
Percutaneous aspiration of the cyst with cytology
Repeat ultrasound in 6 to 12 months
items.explanation: Simple cysts under 5 cm in premenopausal women are almost always benign and usually resolve, and those from 5 to 7 cm warrant follow-up imaging at 6 to 12 months. Surgery is for symptoms, growth, or complex features. Hysterectomy is never indicated for a simple cyst. Aspiration has a high recurrence rate and is not recommended for suspected benign cysts.

items.stem: At laparoscopy for chronic pelvic pain in a 30-year-old woman, which pelvic site is the most common location for endometriosis implants?
options: The sigmoid colon
The umbilicus
The ovaries
The bladder dome
items.explanation: The ovaries, followed by the posterior cul-de-sac and uterosacral ligaments, are the most common sites of endometriosis, and the ovarian form is the endometrioma. Bowel, bladder, and umbilical involvement occur less often and are considered extrapelvic or deep disease sites. Knowing the typical distribution guides inspection at surgery and the interpretation of imaging findings. Knowing the usual distribution guides inspection at surgery.

items.stem: A woman treated with single-dose methotrexate for an ectopic pregnancy has hCG values of 3,800 on day 0, 3,900 on day 4, and 3,500 on day 7. She is stable with mild pain. What is the best next step?
options: A second dose of methotrexate
Laparoscopic salpingectomy
Continued weekly hCG without further treatment
Dilation and curettage under general anesthesia
items.explanation: After single-dose methotrexate, hCG should fall by at least 15 percent between day 4 and day 7. Here the decline is about 10 percent, so the response is inadequate and a second dose is appropriate when she remains stable. Surgery is reserved for rupture, instability, or failure after two doses. Observation alone risks persistent trophoblast. Curettage does not treat a tubal gestation.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman collapses in the emergency department with blood pressure 78/40 mm Hg and heart rate 134. Her urine pregnancy test is positive, and bedside ultrasonography shows free fluid in the hepatorenal space. What is the best management?
options: Intramuscular methotrexate with observation on the ward
Emergent surgery with simultaneous resuscitation
A repeat quantitative hCG measurement in 48 hours
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis first
items.explanation: A positive pregnancy test with shock and intraperitoneal fluid is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise and requires immediate surgery, laparoscopy or laparotomy, with simultaneous fluid and blood resuscitation. Methotrexate is contraindicated in rupture or instability. Repeating a level or obtaining further imaging wastes critical minutes in a patient who is actively bleeding. Every minute of delay increases the chance of death from hemorrhage.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had no menses for 4 months after a curettage for an incomplete abortion. Pregnancy test, FSH, TSH, and prolactin are normal, and there is no withdrawal bleeding after estrogen followed by a progestin. What is the most likely cause?
options: Premature ovarian insufficiency
Hyperprolactinemia
Hypothalamic amenorrhea
Intrauterine adhesions
items.explanation: Amenorrhea after uterine curettage with normal ovarian and pituitary hormones and no withdrawal bleeding after estrogen and progestin indicates an outflow or endometrial problem, most often intrauterine adhesions, or Asherman syndrome. Premature ovarian insufficiency would raise FSH. Hyperprolactinemia is excluded by a normal prolactin. Hypothalamic amenorrhea would give a withdrawal bleed. Hysteroscopy confirms and treats the adhesions.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has sudden left lower quadrant pain. Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL, and she is stable with a normal pulse. Ultrasonography shows a 4 cm ovarian cyst with a small amount of pelvic free fluid and no other abnormality. Which management is appropriate?
options: Immediate oophorectomy
Methotrexate
Observation with analgesia and a repeat hemoglobin
Exploratory laparotomy
items.explanation: A ruptured hemorrhagic or corpus luteum cyst with a small hemoperitoneum in a stable patient with a normal hemoglobin can be managed expectantly with analgesia and repeat hemoglobin checks. Surgery is reserved for instability or a falling hemoglobin. Oophorectomy is not needed for a functional cyst. Methotrexate treats ectopic pregnancy, which should be excluded first with a pregnancy test.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 19 weeks has acute, localized right-sided uterine pain and low-grade fever. She has a known 7 cm intramural fibroid. White count is mildly elevated, and the fetal heart rate is normal. What is the best management?
options: Emergency myomectomy to remove the degenerating fibroid
Uterine artery embolization of the degenerating fibroid
Immediate induction of labor for suspected chorioamnionitis
Hydration, rest, and analgesia as supportive care
items.explanation: Pain with low-grade fever over a known fibroid in the second trimester is typically red degeneration, caused by infarction of a rapidly growing fibroid. It is self-limited and managed with fluids, rest, and analgesia, using NSAIDs only briefly in this gestational window. Surgery during pregnancy is reserved for refractory cases. Embolization is avoided in pregnancy, and delivery is not indicated at 19 weeks.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had burning pain with attempted intercourse and tampon use for 1 year. Cotton-swab touch to the vestibule at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions reproduces the pain. The skin and mucosa appear normal and wet mount and cultures are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Localized provoked vulvodynia (vestibulodynia)
Lichen sclerosus
Candida vulvovaginitis
Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia
items.explanation: Provoked burning pain at the vestibule on light touch with normal-appearing tissue and negative testing defines vulvodynia, here localized provoked. Lichen sclerosus produces visible white, thin, atrophic skin. Candida vulvovaginitis has discharge, erythema, and positive microscopy or culture. Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia causes visible lesions and needs biopsy. Pelvic floor therapy and topical anesthetics are first-line treatment.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a 9 cm tubo-ovarian abscess has received intravenous antibiotics for 72 hours. She remains febrile with persistent pain, but her vital signs are otherwise stable and there is no peritonitis. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to the oral outpatient regimen
Image-guided percutaneous drainage
Continue the same antibiotics for another week without change
Repeat imaging after 2 weeks
items.explanation: Failure to improve within 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics, or a large abscess, calls for drainage, and image-guided percutaneous or transvaginal drainage is minimally invasive and effective in stable patients. Surgery is reserved for rupture or peritonitis. Oral therapy and prolonged unchanged treatment leave the abscess undrained, and a 2-week delay risks rupture and sepsis.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with heavy menses has a normal biopsy and a large fibroid uterus. She asks which treatment has the highest rate of eliminating bleeding permanently. Which option is correct?
options: Endometrial ablation
Tranexamic acid
Uterine artery embolization
Hysterectomy
items.explanation: Hysterectomy is the only option that definitively ends bleeding and eliminates fibroid recurrence. Ablation reduces bleeding but fails in some women, especially with large uterine volume and fibroids. Tranexamic acid works only while taken, and embolization has a risk of recurrent symptoms and later reintervention. The choice must balance finality against surgical risk and her wishes.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with a copper intrauterine device has a clinical diagnosis of mild pelvic inflammatory disease. She wishes to keep the device. Which management is appropriate?
options: Remove the device first and delay antibiotics until it is out
Treat with antibiotics and keep the device in place
Replace the device immediately with a fresh new device
Delay antibiotics until culture results are available
items.explanation: An intrauterine device does not need removal in pelvic inflammatory disease, because outcomes are similar whether it stays or goes, and treatment should not be delayed. If symptoms fail to improve within 48 to 72 hours, removal is considered. Cultures should not delay empiric therapy. Replacing the device during active infection is not recommended. Persistent symptoms at 72 hours should prompt reassessment.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has heavy menses and a normal pelvic examination and ultrasound. Endometrial biopsy is not indicated. She wants a nonhormonal medical option that reduces blood loss only during menses. Which medication is most appropriate?
options: Tranexamic acid
Medroxyprogesterone acetate
Clomiphene citrate
Letrozole
items.explanation: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic taken only on heavy bleeding days and reduces menstrual blood loss without hormones. Medroxyprogesterone is a hormonal progestin. Clomiphene and letrozole induce ovulation and do not treat heavy menstrual bleeding. Tranexamic acid is contraindicated with active thromboembolic disease, so a history of clotting should be checked before prescribing. A history of clotting should be reviewed before prescribing it.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has severe cyclic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea for 2 years that interfere with school. Examination and transvaginal ultrasonography are normal, she is not seeking pregnancy, and she has no contraindication to estrogen. What is the best initial management?
options: Laparoscopy with ablation before any medical therapy
Leuprolide for 12 months without add-back therapy
NSAIDs plus continuous combined hormonal contraception
Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
items.explanation: Endometriosis can be treated empirically, without surgical confirmation, when the picture is typical. First-line therapy is an NSAID with a hormonal method, often given continuously to suppress menses. Surgery is reserved for failure of medical therapy or a mass. A GnRH agonist is a second-line option and needs add-back therapy to protect bone. Hysterectomy is far too aggressive for a young woman.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman is treated with methotrexate for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy. She asks what to avoid during the following weeks. Which instruction is correct?
options: Avoid NSAIDs, folate supplements, and sun exposure
Take ibuprofen as needed and continue prenatal vitamins
Resume intercourse and exercise as soon as pain resolves
Stop follow-up testing once the pain is gone
items.explanation: NSAIDs reduce renal clearance of methotrexate and raise its toxicity, folate supplements can antagonize its action, and sun exposure can cause photosensitivity skin reactions. Pain resolution does not confirm resolution of the pregnancy, so hCG surveillance continues until undetectable, and intercourse and strenuous activity are avoided until then because the tube can still rupture. Pain relief is managed with acetaminophen instead.

items.stem: A 24-year-old sexually active woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain. Temperature is 38.1 C, and she has cervical motion tenderness with mucopurulent discharge. Pregnancy test is negative and she is clinically stable. Which outpatient regimen is recommended?
options: Azithromycin 1 g orally once, with no other antimicrobials added
Ceftriaxone once, plus doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once, with no oral agents afterward
Doxycycline twice daily for 7 days, with no injection or anaerobic coverage
items.explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease needs broad coverage of gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes. The outpatient regimen is a single ceftriaxone injection plus 14 days of doxycycline and metronidazole. Single-dose azithromycin or ceftriaxone alone leaves chlamydia or anaerobes inadequately treated. Seven days of doxycycline alone is too short and omits gonorrhea and anaerobic coverage. Pregnancy must be excluded first, and recent partners need treatment.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is 6 hours after a second-trimester induction abortion with retained placenta. She has heavy bleeding and the placenta has not delivered. What is the best next step?
options: Observation for 24 hours before any intervention is taken
Intravenous antibiotics only, with no removal procedure
Repeat misoprostol and delay surgery for 48 hours
Manual or instrumental removal plus a uterotonic
items.explanation: A retained placenta with heavy bleeding after second-trimester abortion requires prompt removal, either manually or with instruments under ultrasound guidance, along with uterotonic medication and resuscitation as needed. Observation allows ongoing hemorrhage. Antibiotics alone do not control bleeding. Delaying for further misoprostol does not address active blood loss and risks hemodynamic compromise and infection. Retained tissue also raises the risk of infection.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with a missed miscarriage at 9 weeks chooses medical management, and mifepristone is not available. Which misoprostol regimen is recommended?
options: 100 mcg orally once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks
200 mcg vaginally every day for 5 consecutive days
800 mcg vaginally, with one repeat dose in 3 hours
1,600 mcg buccally as a single dose, without repeating
items.explanation: For early pregnancy loss, misoprostol 800 mcg given vaginally is the standard when used alone, and a second dose can be given at least 3 hours later if there is no response, with a high success rate over several days. The other regimens are not recommended doses and use inaccurate intervals or excessive amounts that increase side effects without added benefit.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has chronic pelvic pain, and a hysterectomy 5 years ago at another hospital included bilateral oophorectomy for endometriosis. She now has cyclic pain despite no hormone therapy, and imaging shows a 3 cm pelvic sidewall mass. What is the most likely cause?
options: Pelvic congestion syndrome
Ovarian remnant syndrome
Interstitial cystitis
Residual vulvodynia
items.explanation: Cyclic pain with a pelvic mass after a reported bilateral oophorectomy, especially with a premenopausal hormone profile, points to residual ovarian tissue left at surgery, called ovarian remnant syndrome. Pelvic congestion produces dull pain from dilated veins without a mass. Interstitial cystitis causes bladder symptoms. Vulvodynia is a vulvar pain disorder and would not generate a pelvic sidewall mass.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding and a normal uterine cavity also wants highly effective contraception. Which therapy produces the greatest reduction in menstrual blood loss?
options: Mefenamic acid during menses
Luteal-phase oral progestin only
Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system
Daily iron supplementation alone
items.explanation: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss by roughly 70 to 95 percent and provides contraception, making it the most effective medical option for heavy bleeding without structural disease. NSAIDs lower flow by a smaller fraction. Luteal-phase progestin alone does not control heavy bleeding. Iron treats the anemia that results but does nothing to reduce the bleeding itself.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging 10 cm uterine mass with an irregular margin on imaging and is scheduled for laparoscopic hysterectomy. Which precaution is appropriate?
options: Use power morcellation freely to allow a small incision
Give a GnRH agonist and defer any surgery for a full year to see growth
Perform myomectomy so that the uterus is kept
Avoid power morcellation; remove the specimen intact or contained
items.explanation: Rapid growth of a large mass, particularly after midlife, raises concern for uterine sarcoma, and morcellating an unsuspected sarcoma can spread cancer and worsen prognosis. Intact removal or contained morcellation is advised. Free power morcellation is discouraged in this setting. Deferring treatment delays diagnosis, and myomectomy still involves fragmenting tissue and does not evaluate the lesion adequately.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has 8 months of urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic pain that worsens as the bladder fills and improves after voiding. Urinalysis and culture are negative, and cystoscopy findings are unremarkable. What is the best first-line management?
options: Education, dietary modification, and pelvic floor physical therapy
Bladder instillation with dimethyl sulfoxide as the first treatment
A prolonged course of fluoroquinolone antibiotics for presumed infection
Sacral neuromodulation implantation before conservative measures
items.explanation: Bladder pain syndrome, or interstitial cystitis, is a diagnosis of exclusion, and first-line treatment is conservative: patient education, avoiding bladder irritants, stress reduction, and pelvic floor therapy. Intravesical therapy and neuromodulation are later steps. Antibiotics have no role when cultures are sterile and add resistance risk without benefit. Flares are tracked so that personal triggers can be identified over time.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman at 11 weeks presents for surgical abortion and is Rh negative with a negative antibody screen. Which management of her Rh status is appropriate?
options: No immune globulin, because the pregnancy is under 12 weeks
Anti-D immune globulin only if bleeding exceeds 500 mL
Delay anti-D immune globulin until 28 weeks of the next pregnancy
Anti-D immune globulin at the time of the procedure
items.explanation: An Rh-negative woman who undergoes abortion can be exposed to fetal red cells and should receive anti-D immune globulin at the time of the procedure. Either dose is acceptable in the first trimester. Assuming that early gestation is exempt is outdated. Bleeding volume does not determine the need. Waiting until a future pregnancy leaves alloimmunization from this exposure unprevented.

items.stem: A 36-year-old multiparous woman has had a dull, aching pelvic pain for 8 months that worsens by evening and after prolonged standing, and also aches after intercourse. Imaging shows dilated, tortuous pelvic veins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pelvic congestion syndrome
Pelvic adhesive disease
Endometriosis
Irritable bowel syndrome
items.explanation: Dull pelvic pain that worsens with standing and late in the day, with postcoital aching and dilated pelvic veins on imaging in a parous woman, is characteristic of pelvic congestion syndrome. Adhesions produce positional or localized pain without venous dilation. Endometriosis tends to cause cyclic pain with deep dyspareunia. Irritable bowel syndrome has bowel habit changes and abdominal pain relieved by defecation.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 6 weeks by dates has an hCG of 2,100 mIU/mL, and transvaginal ultrasonography shows no intrauterine or adnexal findings. Two days later, the hCG is 2,350 mIU/mL, and she is stable without pain. What is the best interpretation?
options: The normal rise confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy
The rise is suboptimal and suggests an abnormal pregnancy
The value excludes an ectopic pregnancy
The change is explained by laboratory variation and needs no follow-up
items.explanation: In early viable intrauterine pregnancy with a starting hCG of 1,500 to 3,000, the minimum expected rise over 48 hours is about 40 percent. A rise of only 12 percent is suboptimal and is consistent with an ectopic pregnancy or a failing intrauterine pregnancy. Normal-appearing labs cannot exclude ectopic implantation, and the change is too large to blame on assay variation.

items.stem: A 38-year-old nulligravid woman has heavy cyclic bleeding and has been unable to conceive for 2 years. Saline infusion sonography shows a 3 cm mass that distorts and protrudes into the endometrial cavity. Which fibroid location best explains both complaints?
options: Subserosal on the posterior fundus
Intraligamentous within the broad ligament
Submucosal, projecting into the cavity
Intramural and smaller than 2 cm
items.explanation: Submucosal fibroids distort the cavity, enlarge the endometrial surface area, and impair implantation, so they are tied to heavy bleeding and reduced fertility. Subserosal fibroids tend to cause pressure symptoms rather than bleeding. Intraligamentous fibroids can displace the ureter but do not alter the cavity. Small intramural fibroids that leave the cavity undistorted rarely affect bleeding or conception.

items.stem: A woman has a positive pregnancy test and a transvaginal scan at what she believes is 7 weeks. Which finding alone is diagnostic of a failed pregnancy?
options: A crown-rump length of 4 mm without cardiac activity
Mean sac diameter of 25 mm or more, no embryo
A sac diameter of 16 mm with no yolk sac
An empty sac of 12 mm in diameter
items.explanation: Diagnostic criteria for failed pregnancy include an empty sac with a mean diameter of 25 mm or more, or a crown-rump length of 7 mm or more without cardiac activity. A crown-rump length of 4 mm, a sac of 16 mm without a yolk sac, or a small empty sac are only suspicious findings, and repeat ultrasonography after 7 to 10 days is recommended before acting.

items.stem: One week after taking mifepristone and misoprostol at 8 weeks, a woman reports only light bleeding. Ultrasonography shows an intact gestational sac with cardiac activity. What is the best next step?
options: Reassurance because light bleeding is expected
Repeat mifepristone alone and reassess next week
Methotrexate to end the ongoing pregnancy medically
Aspiration, because the pregnancy is ongoing
items.explanation: Cardiac activity a week after the regimen confirms a continuing pregnancy, meaning medical abortion has failed, and the fetus may have been exposed to the drugs, so the pregnancy should be terminated with aspiration, or counseling about a second misoprostol dose may be offered. Light bleeding is not reassuring here. Mifepristone alone and methotrexate are not accepted methods for this failure.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman passed tissue 2 days ago and now has a fever of 39.2 C, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, and a tender uterus. Her pregnancy test is positive, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. What is the best management?
options: Intravenous antibiotics and prompt uterine evacuation
Oral antibiotics alone with clinic follow-up in 1 week
Expectant management and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug
Methotrexate to resolve retained trophoblast
items.explanation: Fever, foul discharge, and a tender uterus after pregnancy loss indicate septic abortion caused by infected retained products. Treatment is intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, then evacuation of the uterus without delay. Oral therapy alone leaves the infected source in place. Expectant care risks sepsis. Methotrexate is used for ectopic pregnancy, not for infected retained tissue. Delay in evacuation allows sepsis to progress.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has lower abdominal pain, fever, and mucopurulent cervical discharge. She is diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease. Which finding is a criterion for the minimum diagnosis in a sexually active young woman?
options: An elevated serum CA 125 level
A positive pregnancy test
Cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness on examination
A complex adnexal mass on ultrasound
items.explanation: Empiric treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease is recommended in a sexually active young woman with pelvic or lower abdominal pain when cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness is found and no other cause exists. Additional findings such as fever or discharge support the diagnosis. CA 125 is nonspecific. A positive pregnancy test does not define it. An adnexal mass indicates a complication, not the minimum criterion.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a 4 cm adnexal mass on ultrasonography that is anechoic with a thin wall, two thin septations, and no solid areas or flow. She is asymptomatic. What is the best management?
options: Follow-up imaging for benign features
Immediate hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy
Computed tomography-guided biopsy
Chemotherapy before any diagnosis
items.explanation: A cyst with thin septations and no solid component or flow carries a low risk of malignancy and can be followed with repeat ultrasonography, with surgery for symptoms, growth, or developing suspicious features. Radical surgery is excessive without suspicious features. Percutaneous biopsy of a suspected ovarian lesion is avoided because it risks spillage, and chemotherapy has no role without a diagnosis.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a pregnancy test that is positive. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a thin endometrium, no gestational sac, and a small amount of echogenic fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her hCG is 4,500 mIU/mL, and she is stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Complete abortion
Normal early intrauterine pregnancy
Ectopic pregnancy
Molar pregnancy
items.explanation: An hCG above the discriminatory level with an empty uterus and echogenic free fluid is highly suspicious for ectopic pregnancy. A complete abortion would show a falling hCG after tissue passage. A normal intrauterine pregnancy should show a sac at this hCG level. A molar pregnancy typically shows a heterogeneous uterine mass with a very high hCG, not an empty cavity.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman receiving leuprolide for endometriosis has bothersome hot flashes. Which addition best relieves her symptoms and protects bone density without reducing the treatment effect?
options: High-dose unopposed estrogen
Doubling the leuprolide dose
Switching to danazol
Norethindrone acetate 5 mg daily as add-back
items.explanation: Add-back therapy with a low-dose progestin such as norethindrone acetate, with or without a small dose of estrogen, reduces vasomotor symptoms and bone loss while preserving the pain relief from GnRH agonist suppression. High-dose estrogen would stimulate lesions and defeat the therapy. A larger agonist dose worsens the hypoestrogenic state. Danazol has androgenic effects and is not a substitute.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute lower abdominal pain and is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate first laboratory test?
options: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
A urine or serum pregnancy test
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
Diagnostic laparoscopy
items.explanation: In any reproductive-age woman with acute pelvic pain, a pregnancy test comes first because ectopic pregnancy is life-threatening and the result directs imaging and avoids unnecessary radiation. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are premature, and laparoscopy is reserved for instability or inconclusive evaluation. Ultrasonography follows the pregnancy test and clinical examination. Imaging for the cause of pain follows the pregnancy result.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease. Which feature is an indication for hospital admission and parenteral therapy?
options: A positive cervical gonorrhea test
Age younger than 25 years
Pregnancy
A history of prior pelvic infection
items.explanation: Pregnancy is a criterion for hospitalization with pelvic inflammatory disease because infection risks maternal and fetal complications. Other indications are surgical emergencies that cannot be excluded, a tubo-ovarian abscess, severe illness, intolerance of oral therapy, and failure to improve within 72 hours. A positive gonorrhea test, young age, or past infection do not by themselves require admission.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome has 3 menses per year, is not seeking pregnancy, and has a normal pelvic examination. Which management best prevents endometrial hyperplasia?
options: Observation, because no treatment is required
Combined hormonal contraception or periodic progestin withdrawal
Unopposed estrogen replacement
Endometrial ablation
items.explanation: Chronic anovulation exposes the endometrium to unopposed estrogen, increasing the risk of hyperplasia and later cancer, so the lining should be shed or suppressed regularly. Combined hormonal contraception or cyclic progestin does this. Observation leaves the risk unaddressed. Unopposed estrogen makes it worse. Ablation is not appropriate in a young woman who may want pregnancy and does not treat the underlying anovulation.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with minimal endometriosis and 18 months of infertility asks whether suppressing the disease with hormones before trying to conceive will improve her chance of pregnancy. Which statement is accurate?
options: Hormonal suppression does not improve fertility in endometriosis
A 6-month GnRH agonist course roughly doubles natural conception rates
Combined oral contraceptives restore tubal function
Danazol is the preferred fertility treatment
items.explanation: Medical suppression treats pain but does not improve fertility, and it delays attempts at conception, so it should not be used for infertility alone. Surgical treatment of minimal disease may modestly raise pregnancy rates, and assisted reproduction is often used. Contraceptives and GnRH agonists do not repair tubal function. Danazol has significant androgenic effects and is not a fertility therapy.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with a 9 cm leiomyoma and hemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL is scheduled for myomectomy in 3 months. What is the main benefit of preoperative GnRH agonist therapy?
options: Permanent cure with no regrowth once treatment is discontinued
Long-term single-agent therapy for 2 years without add-back
Protection against fibroid growth during later pregnancy
Short-term shrinkage and amenorrhea to correct anemia
items.explanation: A GnRH agonist induces a hypoestrogenic state that shrinks fibroids and stops menses, so it is used for about 3 months before surgery to raise hemoglobin and reduce uterine size. Fibroids regrow after therapy ends, so it is not curative. Use beyond 6 months without add-back risks bone loss. It has no role in pregnancy, because treatment is incompatible with conception.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a 5 cm adnexal cyst that is echogenic with a bright nodule, acoustic shadowing, and a fat-fluid level. Doppler shows no internal flow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Mature cystic teratoma
Hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst
Serous cystadenoma
Endometrioma
items.explanation: A cyst with a bright echogenic nodule, acoustic shadowing, and a fat-fluid level is the classic picture of a mature cystic teratoma, or dermoid, which contains fat, hair, and other tissues. A hemorrhagic cyst shows a reticular pattern and resolves. A serous cystadenoma is anechoic with thin septations. An endometrioma has homogeneous ground-glass echoes. Cystectomy with ovarian preservation is typical when symptomatic.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman had an uncomplicated aspiration abortion at 8 weeks and wants contraception. She has no medical conditions. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Waiting 6 weeks before starting any contraceptive method
Delaying an intrauterine device until the next menses
Immediate start of any method, including an IUD
Avoiding hormonal methods for 3 months
items.explanation: Ovulation can return within about 2 weeks after first-trimester abortion, so contraception should start immediately, and an intrauterine device or implant can be placed at the time of the procedure with high continuation and low complication rates. Waiting 6 weeks or for menses leaves her unprotected. Hormonal methods have no required delay after an uncomplicated abortion.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with chronic pelvic pain has a 5 cm unilocular endometrioma with ground-glass echoes on ultrasonography. Medical therapy has failed, and she plans to try to conceive later. Which surgical approach has the lowest recurrence rate?
options: Simple drainage of the cyst contents only
Cystectomy with excision of the cyst wall
Oophorectomy of the entire affected ovary
Aspiration of the cyst under ultrasound guidance
items.explanation: Excision of the endometrioma wall lowers recurrence of both cysts and pain and improves spontaneous pregnancy rates compared with drainage or ablation alone, although counseling about possible ovarian reserve reduction is needed. Drainage and aspiration leave the lining behind, so the cyst returns quickly. Oophorectomy removes more tissue than necessary in a patient who wants future fertility.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has severe deep dyspareunia and painful defecation during menses. Examination reveals a tender nodule in the rectovaginal septum. Which imaging study best defines the extent of suspected deep disease?
options: Plain abdominal radiography
Serum CA 125 measurement
Hysterosalpingography
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
items.explanation: Deep infiltrating endometriosis involving the rectovaginal septum, bowel, or ureters is best mapped by pelvic magnetic resonance imaging or expert transvaginal ultrasonography, which helps plan surgery. Plain films show no useful detail. CA 125 can rise in many conditions and does not define extent. Hysterosalpingography evaluates the cavity and tubes, not deep pelvic lesions. Surgeons rely on the imaging map to plan bowel and ureteral involvement.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 10 weeks has sudden severe left lower quadrant pain and vomiting. Ultrasonography shows a viable intrauterine pregnancy and a 7 cm left ovarian mass with an enlarged ovary and decreased flow. What is the best management?
options: Laparoscopic detorsion
Termination of the pregnancy before surgery
Left oophorectomy as the standard approach
Observation until the second trimester
items.explanation: Suspected torsion in pregnancy is a surgical emergency, and laparoscopic detorsion is safe in any trimester and preserves the ovary, including the corpus luteum that supports early pregnancy. Terminating the pregnancy is unnecessary. Routine oophorectomy sacrifices a salvageable ovary. Waiting risks infarction and loss of the ovary, so treatment should not be postponed. The ovary has a good chance of full recovery after prompt surgery.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has had heavy menses lasting 9 days with every cycle since menarche at age 12. She also has frequent nosebleeds, and her mother has required iron infusions for heavy periods. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with a normal platelet count. Which laboratory evaluation is most appropriate next?
options: Prothrombin time and international normalized ratio alone
Von Willebrand antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, and factor VIII
Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutation testing
Antithrombin and protein C activity levels
items.explanation: Heavy bleeding since menarche with mucosal bleeding and a family history suggests an inherited bleeding disorder, and von Willebrand disease is the most common. Testing includes antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, and factor VIII. A prothrombin time alone misses it. Factor V Leiden, antithrombin, and protein C evaluate thrombophilia, which causes clotting rather than bleeding. Treatment is then guided by the hematology results.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has an unruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy and needs surgery. Her right tube was removed for a previous ectopic pregnancy, and she wants future fertility. Which surgical approach is most appropriate?
options: Left salpingectomy only, removing the affected tube
Bilateral salpingectomy to prevent recurrence
Hysterectomy to prevent any further ectopic pregnancy
Left salpingostomy with weekly hCG follow-up
items.explanation: When the contralateral tube is absent or damaged and fertility is desired, salpingostomy is considered to preserve the only tube, accepting a risk of persistent trophoblast that requires hCG surveillance and possible methotrexate. Salpingectomy of the remaining tube would eliminate natural conception. Bilateral salpingectomy and hysterectomy are not indicated for a single ectopic gestation. Surgery is therefore tailored to preserve her only tube.

items.stem: Twelve hours after an uncomplicated suction procedure at 10 weeks, a 25-year-old woman has heavy bleeding. The uterus is soft and enlarged, and ultrasonography shows an empty cavity. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate hysterectomy for uncontrolled uterine bleeding
Repeat pelvic ultrasonography in 24 hours to reassess
Uterine massage and administration of a uterotonic
Observation until the bleeding stops on its own accord
items.explanation: A soft, enlarged uterus with an empty cavity and brisk bleeding indicates atony, the most common cause of hemorrhage after abortion. First-line treatment is bimanual massage with a uterotonic such as oxytocin or methylergonovine, then misoprostol or tranexamic acid. Hysterectomy is a last resort. Delay or observation allows continued blood loss in an actively bleeding patient.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman develops sudden severe right lower quadrant pain with vomiting. Ultrasonography shows a 6 cm ovarian cyst, and Doppler flow to the ovary is present. Her vital signs are stable. What is the best management?
options: Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian preservation
Right oophorectomy with salpingectomy to remove the cyst
Observation with repeat Doppler flow study in 6 hours
Oral contraceptives to suppress further cyst growth
items.explanation: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis, and present Doppler flow does not exclude it because dual blood supply can preserve flow. Prompt laparoscopic detorsion usually restores function even when the ovary looks dusky, so conservation is preferred in a young woman. Oophorectomy is reserved for suspected malignancy. Waiting risks necrosis, and hormonal suppression does not untwist an adnexa.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 12 weeks has a known 6 cm intramural fibroid and asks about risks for the rest of her pregnancy. Which counseling statement is accurate?
options: Fibroids carry no increased risks for the pregnancy or delivery
Myomectomy is required in the second trimester of pregnancy
Fibroids raise the risk of malpresentation and cesarean
Vaginal birth is absolutely contraindicated
items.explanation: Fibroids are associated with a higher chance of fetal malpresentation, preterm birth, placental abruption, postpartum hemorrhage, and cesarean delivery, but most women with them have uncomplicated pregnancies. Myomectomy during pregnancy is not routine and is avoided because of bleeding risk. Vaginal birth is not contraindicated unless a fibroid obstructs the birth canal. Individual counseling should reflect the fibroid location and size.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has not menstruated for 14 months and now has light vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. What is the best next step?
options: Reassurance and annual follow-up
Endometrial sampling
A 3-month trial of oral progestin
Repeat ultrasonography in 6 months
items.explanation: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation for endometrial cancer, and an endometrial thickness above 4 mm in this setting calls for tissue sampling. Reassurance would miss a potential malignancy. A progestin trial treats presumed hyperplasia without a diagnosis. Waiting 6 months delays evaluation of a high-risk symptom. A thickness of 4 mm or less can sometimes be followed, but this patient does not meet it.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has intermenstrual spotting for 5 months. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a focal, echogenic endometrial lesion with a single feeding vessel on color Doppler. Hemoglobin is normal. What is the best next step?
options: Endometrial ablation
Treatment with a GnRH agonist
Observation for a year with annual ultrasound
Hysteroscopic polypectomy
items.explanation: A focal echogenic lesion with a feeding vessel is typical of an endometrial polyp, and symptomatic polyps in a woman near menopause should be removed under direct visualization to relieve bleeding and obtain tissue to exclude malignancy. Ablation would destroy the lining without removing the lesion or providing a diagnosis. A GnRH agonist does not cure polyps. Prolonged observation delays a tissue diagnosis in a symptomatic woman.

items.stem: A 40-year-old G2P2 woman with a 12 cm submucosal and intramural fibroid and severe anemia wishes to avoid surgery, and she has completed childbearing. She has no contraindication to angiography. Which minimally invasive option is appropriate?
options: Endometrial ablation
Uterine artery embolization
Dilation and curettage
Cervical cerclage placement
items.explanation: Uterine artery embolization shrinks fibroids by blocking their blood supply and suits women who want to avoid surgery and have completed childbearing. Ablation treats the lining and is poorly effective with large submucosal fibroids that distort the cavity. Curettage does not address the mass. Cerclage is a pregnancy procedure and has no role in managing fibroids.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman has a fibroid uterus of 14 weeks size with heavy bleeding, completed childbearing, and normal cervical screening. She requests definitive treatment and prefers the least invasive route. Which surgical approach is generally preferred?
options: Open abdominal hysterectomy through a midline incision
Supracervical hysterectomy through a midline incision
Laparotomy with myomectomy rather than hysterectomy
Minimally invasive hysterectomy, vaginal if feasible
items.explanation: When hysterectomy is chosen for benign disease, the vaginal route is preferred when feasible, then laparoscopic, because of faster recovery and fewer complications than abdominal surgery. A 14-week fibroid uterus is often removable by a minimally invasive approach. Myomectomy preserves the uterus, which does not fit her request for definitive treatment. Leaving the cervix is optional and does not define the route.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl with known type 1 von Willebrand disease has heavy bleeding that has lasted 10 days. Her hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL, and she is hemodynamically stable. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily during menses to reduce flow
Daily aspirin to lessen flow and reduce clot formation
Tranexamic acid with or without desmopressin, plus hormones
Dilation and curettage under general anesthesia
items.explanation: Heavy bleeding in a patient with von Willebrand disease is treated with antifibrinolytic therapy such as tranexamic acid, desmopressin to raise von Willebrand factor in responsive patients, and hormonal therapy to suppress the endometrium, with hematology involvement. NSAIDs and aspirin impair platelet function and can worsen bleeding. Curettage is not appropriate, because it does not correct a coagulation defect.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had heavy vaginal bleeding for 3 weeks, soaking a pad every hour today. Hemoglobin is 7.5 g/dL, pregnancy test is negative, and vital signs are stable. Ultrasonography shows a normal uterus. Which acute treatment is most appropriate?
options: Intravenous conjugated estrogen every 4 to 6 hours
Oral norethindrone 0.35 mg once daily until bleeding stops
Immediate hysterectomy to achieve definitive control of bleeding
Dilation and curettage as the first step in treatment
items.explanation: Acute heavy anovulatory bleeding in a stable adolescent responds to high-dose estrogen, which promotes endometrial growth and hemostasis, followed by a progestin or combined pill to stabilize the lining. A low-dose progestin-only tablet is too weak for acute bleeding. Hysterectomy is inappropriate in a young patient. Curettage is reserved for failure of medical therapy or instability.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman reports heavy menses for 8 months with fatigue. Vital signs and pelvic examination are normal. Which initial laboratory evaluation is most appropriate?
options: Karyotype analysis
Serum estradiol and luteinizing hormone
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
Pregnancy test and complete blood count
items.explanation: The initial evaluation of heavy menstrual bleeding is a pregnancy test and a complete blood count to exclude pregnancy complications and quantify anemia, with thyroid testing and bleeding disorder screening added by history. Karyotyping and hormone levels are not routine and do not alter first-line management. Imaging begins with ultrasonography when examination or history suggests a structural cause, not magnetic resonance imaging.

items.stem: Three days after uterine artery embolization for symptomatic fibroids, a 41-year-old woman has pelvic cramping, nausea, and a temperature of 37.9 C. White cell count is 12,000 per microliter, and she is otherwise well. What is the best management?
options: Emergency hysterectomy for presumed uterine necrosis
Immediate intravenous vancomycin for presumed sepsis
Supportive analgesia and antiemetics
Repeat embolization of the uterine arteries now
items.explanation: Pain, low-grade fever, nausea, and mild leukocytosis within days of embolization represent post-embolization syndrome, caused by fibroid ischemia, and are managed supportively with analgesia, antiemetics, and hydration. Hysterectomy is for uterine necrosis or sepsis, which would show high fever, severe pain, or foul discharge. Antibiotics are not needed without infection signs, and repeat embolization has no role.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 9 weeks has heavy vaginal bleeding with cramping. She has passed some tissue, and examination shows an open cervical os with additional tissue visible at the os. Which classification of early pregnancy loss best fits?
options: Threatened abortion
Incomplete abortion
Complete abortion
Missed abortion
items.explanation: An open os with passage of some products of conception and tissue remaining at the os is an incomplete abortion. A threatened abortion has bleeding with a closed os and a viable pregnancy. A complete abortion means all tissue has passed, the os is typically closed, and bleeding has lessened. A missed abortion is a nonviable pregnancy retained without bleeding or passage of tissue.

items.stem: During a suction evacuation at 8 weeks, the surgeon notes that the instrument passed much deeper than expected, and omentum is seen in the aspirated tissue. The patient is currently stable. What is the best next step?
options: Laparoscopy or laparotomy to look for bowel injury
Complete the evacuation and discharge the patient home
Observation in the recovery area overnight alone
Methylergonovine and routine discharge the same day
items.explanation: Visible omentum or bowel in the specimen after a deep pass indicates uterine perforation with possible visceral injury, and the abdomen must be explored, usually laparoscopically, to look for bowel or vascular damage. Continuing the procedure risks further injury. Overnight observation or uterotonics alone can miss a bowel injury, which can become fatal if unrecognized.

items.stem: A 43-year-old G3P3 woman has progressively heavy, painful menses. The uterus is symmetrically enlarged, globular, and tender at the time of her period. Ultrasonography shows a uterus of 10 weeks size with normal ovaries and no discrete mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Multiple intramural leiomyomas
Endometrial polyp
Complex endometrial hyperplasia
Adenomyosis
items.explanation: A diffusely enlarged, globular, tender uterus in a parous woman in her forties with heavy, painful menses is the classic description of adenomyosis, in which endometrial glands lie within the myometrium. Leiomyomas typically produce an irregular, nodular contour with discrete masses. A polyp causes intermenstrual spotting without uterine enlargement. Hyperplasia causes bleeding but not a tender, globular uterus.

items.stem: A 44-year-old G3P3 woman has heavy menses that have failed medical therapy. Her endometrial biopsy is benign, the cavity is normal, and she has completed childbearing. She is considering endometrial ablation. Which counseling point is essential?
options: Reliable contraception is needed because pregnancy is hazardous
Amenorrhea is expected in every patient who undergoes ablation
Future evaluation of bleeding for endometrial cancer is no longer needed
Fertility is unchanged and the procedure is reversible
items.explanation: Ablation destroys the endometrium, and pregnancy that occurs afterward carries high risks of miscarriage, abnormal placentation, and poor outcomes, so effective contraception is mandatory. Many women become amenorrheic, but not all. Ablation does not remove cancer risk, and later bleeding still needs evaluation. The procedure is not reversible and is intended only for women who have completed childbearing.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 19 weeks requests termination of pregnancy by dilation and evacuation. Which measure best reduces the risk of cervical laceration and uterine perforation at this gestational age?
options: Immediate mechanical dilation under general anesthesia without preparation
An oxytocin infusion for 12 hours before the procedure begins
Osmotic dilators or misoprostol for cervical preparation
Prophylactic placement of a cervical cerclage at the start of the case
items.explanation: Second-trimester evacuation requires wider dilation than the first trimester, and preoperative cervical preparation with osmotic dilators, misoprostol, or mifepristone softens the cervix and lowers the risk of laceration and perforation. Forced mechanical dilation alone increases injury. Oxytocin does not ripen the cervix in this setting. A cerclage would prevent dilation and is the opposite of the goal.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has severe pain during the first 2 days of every period, beginning 6 months after menarche. Examination and ultrasound are normal. Which pathophysiologic mechanism best explains primary dysmenorrhea?
options: Retrograde menstruation through the fallopian tubes into the pelvis
Excess endometrial prostaglandins causing uterine contractions
Ectopic endometrial glands growing within the uterine muscle wall
Elevated serum prolactin from a pituitary microadenoma lesion
items.explanation: Primary dysmenorrhea results from prostaglandin F2 alpha and other prostaglandins released by the secretory endometrium, which cause strong uterine contractions and ischemic pain. This is why NSAIDs, which inhibit cyclooxygenase, work well. Retrograde menstruation is linked to endometriosis. Myometrial glands define adenomyosis. High prolactin disrupts ovulation and does not cause dysmenorrhea. This explains the dramatic relief that anti-inflammatory therapy gives.
